title: The API, the CLI and artifacts
summary: Forty-one routes hang off one net/http pattern mux; the role each needs is chosen at registration in internal/api/router.go, not inside the handler, so no endpoint can exist without a level. Every non-2xx body is the same envelope, and two of its codes are load-bearing: 410 fenced means the lease is gone and the job must abort, 503 transient means the database did not answer and the lease is untouched — conflating them is STF #663. That authorisation can be turned on now: cmd/farmd/roles.go asks api.AuthenticatorFor, which reads FARM_API_TOKENS and refuses to start an exposed listener with no credentials rather than booting open. What is still only a promise is the fence — the API bumps it on a revoke and cooperating clients honour it, but the proxy that would enforce it at the ADB socket is not written, and the revoke response says otherwise in so many words.

sections.heading: How a request is shaped, and what comes back
sections.body:
Base path is `/api/v1`. Routing is Go's pattern mux — method is part of the pattern, path variables read with `r.PathValue` — with no third-party router (`router.go:16-26`).

Every non-2xx body is `{"error":{"code","message","detail?}}` and nothing else (`errors.go:26-33`). **`code` is the field you branch on, not the status**, because two of this API's most important failures share a status with unrelated conditions: 409 is both `no_capacity` (ordinary scheduling) and `disruption_refused` (a refusal a human must read).

Every response carries `X-Request-Id` — echoed verbatim if you send one, minted otherwise — and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. A 503 additionally carries `Retry-After: 2` (`errors.go:163-168`).

JSON bodies reject unknown fields (`router.go:309-338`). This is deliberate: silently ignoring a typo like `max_runtime_sec` produces a job with **no** maximum runtime — the difference between a lease that ends on the clock the user wrote down and one that runs until a human notices. Bodies are capped at 1 MiB (`server.go:65`); over that you get 413.

There is no 405. A wrong method falls through to the `/api/v1/` catch-all and reads as a 404 whose message names the method you used. A bare `/api/v1` with no trailing slash gets a 307 from the mux to `/api/v1/`, which then 404s.
bullets: `X-Request-Id` appears in the access log line for the same request, and in ctl's error text — quote it in a ticket.
Panics are recovered into a 500 with the standard envelope; the stack goes to the log, never the body (`router.go:145-168`).
Metric route labels use the matched pattern (`GET /api/v1/leases/{id}/renew`), so cardinality is bounded by the routing table, not by ids clients send (`router.go:231-238`).
`instrument` wraps `recoverer`, not the other way round, so a panicking request still produces an access log line, a 500 in the counter, and a balanced in-flight gauge (`router.go:113-118`).

sections.heading: Every route, with the role it needs
sections.source: internal/api/router.go:33-116 (authoritative), internal/api/artifacts.go:119-132 (contributed at build time via WithRoutes)
sections.body:
Roles are ordered: `tenant` < `operator` < `admin` (`internal/api/auth.go:41-72`). An unknown role ranks 0 and satisfies nothing. An operator route is one that **can take a device away from a running job or disturb hardware somebody else is using**; each writes `farm.audit_log` with the caller's subject.

The artifact block is not in `router.go`. It is contributed by the parent through `api.WithRoutes` (`cmd/farmd/roles.go:132-145`) because the blob backend is a deployment choice. **If the store cannot open, those five routes silently do not exist** and every push/install step fails at its first artifact — the binary logs a WARN at startup and carries on.

Status codes below are what I got hitting each route on the live system, not what the handler could theoretically return.

rows: Liveness. Deliberately does not touch Postgres — killing the API because the database hiccuped widens the very control-plane gap the reaper has to refund.
Readiness: 2 s pool ping (`server.go:85`), plus pool stats.
What this deployment can actually do, observed not declared.
Check a spec. 200 with `valid:false` for a bad spec — but 400 if the body is not a JSON object at all.
200; 400 on an empty or non-object body
The step vocabulary, assert operators, limits.
Expand a reset tier into the exact shell commands. `?profile=` required, `?tier=` optional.
One device. `{id}` is a uuid **or** a `farm_uid`, never an ADB serial.
One shell command at a physical devpath. Touches no lease.
200; 400 empty command; 404 unknown device; 409 device is leased
Hosts with `live_leases` — what a drain would have to wait out.
Request a tier-4 port power cycle. Decides and records; a host agent would switch VBUS.
202 accepted; 409 `disruption_refused`; 409 `conflict` (no controllable power domain); 400 non-integer id; 404 unknown slot
File a job row. Nothing is scheduled here.
One job plus its lease history. Exactly two keys, `job` and `leases`. **No step results.**
End a job, releasing its live lease with reason `job_cancelled` in the same transaction.
Idempotent on `job_id`. Re-attach returns the SAME fence.
The hot path. See the next section.
A human takes a device back. No fence required.
The ladder, recent attempts, open quarantines. `?device= &host= &limit=` (1–1000, default 100).
One command across a selector, capped per hub.
One run and every target's outcome.
Server-Sent Events. **Not tenant-scoped, and cannot be.**
Streamed upload; metadata in the query string.
Forget one digest. `?reason=` lands in the audit log.
Catch-all: a typo gets the JSON envelope, not the dashboard's HTML.

sections.heading: The status codes that carry meaning
sections.body:
Four outcomes decide whether a holder aborts, retries, or does nothing. Get these wrong and you have rebuilt STF #663.

**410 + `fenced`** — `farm.lease_renew` returned zero rows (`leases.go:359-366`). Terminal. Exactly three things produce it: the lease was released, it was reclaimed, or another `acquire` on the same `job_id` re-attached and replaced the `holder_instance`. None of them is a network event. Abort the job, close every ADB socket, write nothing further. Retrying is an attempt to drive a device that now belongs to another job.

**503 + `transient`** — the database did not answer: dial failure, statement timeout, failover, exhausted pool, SQLSTATE 40001/40P01/55P03/57P03/53300/53400 (`errors.go:286-305`). This proves **nothing** about the lease. No deadline moved. Retry with backoff and do not abort. `Retry-After: 2` is set.

**409 + `no_capacity`** — not an error. No healthy, enabled, unleased device matched. Re-queue.

**400 + `check_violation`** — Postgres refused the write against a CHECK. The canonical case is a release reason the schema has no word for. `farm.leases.release_reason` has no connectivity vocabulary, so a socket error cannot end a lease *even if the holder asks it to*. The 400 body lists the seven words that would have worked and names the constraint that fired.

The split is counted separately in `farm_lease_renew_failures_total{kind=fenced|transient}`. On this farm right now that reads `fenced 562, transient 0`.

One more you will see in logs but never as a response: **499 `client_closed`**. The caller hung up. Recorded so an abandoned renewal is not counted as the 200 the status recorder optimistically starts at — on the renewal route that would make a holder whose pod died indistinguishable from one whose lease was renewed (`router.go:281-295`).

sections.heading: acquire, renew, release, revoke
sections.body:
**acquire** (`leases.go:208`) is idempotent on `job_id`, and that is load-bearing. A pod eviction — node drain, preemption, spot reclaim, OOM restart — is the most ordinary event in a Kubernetes control plane and must never cost a device. The replacement calls with the same `job_id` and receives the same lease, the same device and **the same fence**, with `"reattached": true`. Bumping the fence would fence the job out of its own detached work.

Re-attach is an `UPDATE` that overwrites `holder`, overwrites `holder_instance`, and increments `holder_epoch` (`migrations/00002_lease.sql:214-226`). Two consequences an operator should hold on to: the previous process's renewals start returning 410 **at an unchanged fence**, and anyone who knows a `job_id` can perform that takeover. On this demo the job runner does exactly this to any job you create, within about a second.

`farm.lease_acquire` also does not look at `farm.jobs.state`. Acquiring against a cancelled or finished job succeeds and hands out a device; the job runner's `preflight` (`internal/jobrunner/jobrunner.go:783-817`) is what catches it afterwards. If you need a lease that nothing else will steal — to test a refusal path, say — file a job, cancel it, then acquire.

If you omit `holder_instance` the server mints one and returns it with `holder_instance_minted: true`. **You must renew with exactly that value** (`leases.go:227-243`).

**release** passes your reason to Postgres verbatim, with no client-side allow-list (`leases.go:417-430`). That is why the refusal above is a real database CHECK and not a Go `switch` somebody could edit. A release that matched nothing returns **200 with `released:false`** — a fenced holder tidying up lands here and must not be told to retry. A tenant-scoped caller may release only its own tenant's lease (`leases.go:441-475`); that check does nothing under AllowAll and does not separate two clients inside one tenant.

`rearm_ms` may only **lengthen** the slot quarantine, never shorten it (`leases.go:476-495`). `internal/config` asserts at startup that the configured rearm exceeds the node proxy's self-fence timeout; honouring a smaller value from a request body would step around that assertion and hand the slot to the next job while the previous holder's sockets were still open.

**revoke** is the only path where the decision is a person's. It is operator-only, requires no fence — an operator has no reason to know the holder's, and a revoke that needs it fails exactly when it is needed most — is audited with the human's name and reason, and raises `farm.devices.fence_floor` past the revoked fence (`leases.go:656-661`). Both the API body and ctl say the old holder is then "refused at the host proxy". **There is no host proxy in this build** — see gaps. Today the raised floor is enforced in PostgreSQL and honoured by cooperating clients; the slot rearm is what actually buys the time.

sections.heading: Operator routes: what refuses, and why
sections.body:
**drain** changes `farm.hosts.admin_state` and nothing else. The response tells you what you are now waiting on: `live_leases` and `protected_leases`. It says explicitly in the body that nothing was released. `undrain` returns the same shape without the note.

**slot power** is the one that surprises people. On a hub without per-port switching every port shares one power domain, so "power-cycle this slot" is really "power-cycle these seven devices". The handler reads the tier's `requires_policy` from `farm.recovery_tiers` (`ops.go:566-567`, not hard-coded), compares it against every live lease in the blast radius, and **refuses with 409 `disruption_refused` naming the offenders** — lease, job, tenant, holder, policy, rack slot. An unknown `disruption_policy` ranks 0, below `no_disruption`, and refuses: allowing a cycle you should have refused costs somebody's six-hour run; refusing one you could have allowed costs minutes (`ops.go:462-476`).

On success it returns **202**, not 200. The API does not toggle VBUS — it records a `farm.recovery_attempts` row at tier 4 and a host agent consumes it. No host agent is beating on this deployment, so the row sits at `requested` and nothing is switched. The 202 body does not say so; `GET /api/v1/capabilities` does.

**device exec** runs at `slots.adb_devpath`, **never a serial** (`fleet.go:464-471`). Duplicate OEM serials are real — `/api/v1/fleet` marks them `serial_ambiguous: true` — and a serial-addressed exec lands on a different phone than the one on screen. It refuses with 409 on a leased device unless you pass `"force": true` **and** a reason, and it touches no lease either way.

**bulk** caps concurrency per hub (default 4, max 32). That is not politeness: sixty devices answering at once browns out a power domain and manufactures a wave of transport errors indistinguishable from a hardware fault (`ops.go:1063-1068`). Leased devices are skipped by default and recorded as `skipped`.

sections.heading: The SSE stream
sections.body:
`GET /api/v1/stream` is `text/event-stream`. One poller reads the database every 2 s (`server.go:71`) **only while at least one client is connected** and fans diffs out to everyone: ten dashboards cost the same queries as one. A client that cannot keep up is disconnected after 64 queued events, never waited on — blocking the poller on one slow reader would stall every other client while holding a pool connection.

Headers are set before the first flush (order matters; flushing first commits a sniffed 200 and silently discards `Content-Type`): `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` — nginx buffers proxied responses by default, which turns a live stream into a very slow file download.

The first frame is `: connected` plus `retry: 3000`, so a browser dropped for falling behind returns in 3 s with a fresh snapshot.

**Five event names, and nothing else**: `fleet`, `lease`, `job`, `recovery`, `alert`. Each payload is either `{"snapshot":true, ...}` (on connect, and every 30 s) or `{"changed":[...]}` / `{"removed":[...]}` (deltas). A `: heartbeat` comment frame every 15 s defeats proxy idle timeouts.

The **diff key** excludes deadlines, not the payload: `leaseDigest.digestKey()` zeroes `ExpiresUnix` before comparing (`stream.go:339-345`), so a routine heartbeat is not an event, while every lease frame still carries the current `expires_at_unix`.

`alert` kinds, all nine derived rather than stored: `lease_suspect`, `lease_self_healed`, `lease_reclaimed`, `lease_revoked`, `hub_correlation`, `hub_recovered`, `recovery_refused`, `protected_lease_suspect`, `control_plane_gap`. Read the `lease_suspect` message carefully — **suspect is an alert and nothing else**: no reset, no reboot, no reallocation, and a heartbeat in the grace band restores it at the same fence.

The stream is one shared snapshot fanned out to every client, so it carries no tenant filter and cannot be given one without rebuilding the poller per tenant. See gaps.

sections.heading: ctl — the operator command line
sections.body:
`farmd ctl <command>`. It opens **no database connection** — `internal/ctl` imports neither `pgx` nor `database/sql` — and holds no credential Postgres would accept. Every command is an HTTP request against the same `/api/v1` any client uses. That is a constraint, not layering: an operator tool with a private path into the schema is a tool whose refusals can be walked around by the person most likely to be in a hurry at 3am. The single exception is `ctl validate`, which parses locally with the same `internal/jobspec` the server runs.

**Configuration**, in precedence order: flag → loaded config → environment → compiled-in default (`ctl.go:500-520`).
`--url` / `$FARM_API_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:8080`), `--token` / `$FARM_API_TOKEN`, `-o|--output table|json`, `--timeout` (default 30 s).
The HTTP client itself carries **no** timeout (`ctl.go:135-173`) — the event stream and an artifact upload would be severed mid-flight. Ordinary requests get a per-call context deadline instead.

**Destructive commands** (`job cancel`, `lease revoke`, `host drain/undrain`, `device exec`, `bulk`) require `--reason`, print exactly what they are about to disturb with rack positions first, then ask. With no terminal on stdin — a pipe, or `< /dev/null`, which an instant EOF distinguishes from a real terminal — there is nobody to ask, so they refuse unless `--yes` was passed.

**Exit codes**, all four verified: `0` did what it said, `1` failed, `2` bad invocation, `3` the remote **refused** (HTTP 409). 3 is separate from 1 because a refusal is an answer. A script that retries on 1 and stops on 3 does not fight the farm. One overload to know about: `ctl bulk` exits **1** when any target errored, even though the run itself completed and no lease was affected (`commands.go:2050`). Read the run's own `ok/errors/skipped` line, not the exit status, to decide whether the fleet is in trouble.

If a destructive write's reply never arrives, ctl says the outcome is **UNKNOWN**, retries nothing, and names the read that settles it (`ctl.go:606-627`). Re-sending a write that ends somebody's run is not a decision this tool makes on a socket error. A `*RemoteError` passes through untouched, because there the server answered and the state is known.

`-o json` emits the API's own response body verbatim, re-indented — so a script parses the API's schema, not a second one ctl invented.

sections.heading: Artifacts: content addressing and why it matters at 60 devices
sections.body:
A spec that says "push `/builds/nightly/app.apk`" is a promise about a filesystem the runner cannot keep. A spec that names `sha256:9f2b…` names the content, and the farm can then answer the only question that matters at provisioning time — *are these exact bytes already on that device?* — without transferring anything.

**The arithmetic**: a 200 MB APK pushed to 60 devices is 12 GB over USB. Pushed once and skipped 59 times it is 200 MB. `farm.device_artifacts` is the ledger that permits the skip and `EnsureOnDevice` is the only thing that reads and writes it (`store.go:12-16, 863`).

**Upload** is the body and nothing else — no multipart, no base64, no JSON envelope. Every one of those puts a framing layer between the socket and the disk, and this endpoint's whole job is to move several hundred megabytes without ever holding them. Metadata rides in the query string: `kind` (apk, file, script, bundle), `name`, optional `sha256`.

The declared `sha256` is **not** how the artifact is named — the digest is computed regardless. It is how you prove the transfer was faithful, and it is verified **inside the stream**, not after (`artifacts.go:355-395`). After would be too late: `Store.Put` publishes the bytes and writes `farm.artifacts` before it returns, so a post-hoc check would have to delete a row and orphan a blob it just created. Failing the read instead makes Put's own error path do the work — staged bytes aborted, no row written, farm exactly as it was. Only a clean EOF triggers the comparison, so a truncated upload surfaces as its own transport error rather than as "your file is wrong".

**Bytes are committed before the row** (`store.go:640-668`). An orphaned blob with no row is harmless garbage a later Put of identical content adopts; a row pointing at bytes that are not there is a promise the farm cannot keep. `Commit` fsyncs, then renames within the same filesystem — staging lives under the blob root, not `os.TempDir` — so a crash before the rename leaves a nameless staging file and after it leaves complete content. The dangerous state, a truncated file under a digest that vouches for it, is unreachable.

**DELETE is operator-only and refuses whenever anything still names the content.** `farm.device_artifacts.sha256` is `ON DELETE CASCADE` (`migrations/00004_operate.sql:137`), so an unguarded delete takes the ledger rows with it and the fleet quietly forgets that sixty phones already hold this build — then re-pushes 200 MB to all of them. A terminal job's reference blocks too: deleting content a finished run installed destroys the only record of what it ran. The row is locked `FOR UPDATE` first, which conflicts with the `FOR KEY SHARE` a new ledger insert takes, so no device can start holding it mid-check. The reference scan has a 15 s deadline and **fails closed** — a timeout refuses the delete, never permits one (`artifacts.go:599-606`).

The blob is **not** removed. `artifacts.Backend` has three methods — Create, Open, URL (`store.go:222-235`) — and no verb for removal, by design: content addressing means an unreferenced blob is inert, a later identical upload adopts it, and reclaiming disk is a sweep, not a side effect of an HTTP request. The response says so in `blob_retained: true` rather than implying it. Nothing ships that does the sweep — see gaps.

Blob root is `$FARM_ARTIFACT_DIR`, defaulting to `<tmp>/device-farmer-artifacts`, fanned out one level by the first two hex characters (`cmd/farmd/roles.go:383-396`, `store.go:243-276`).

sections.heading: EnsureOnDevice: the skip, and what a failed push does not cost you
sections.body:
The sequence, and why it is in this order:

1. Read the artifact row and the device's ledger row **together**. An unknown digest or a malformed device id fails here, before anything touches the device.
2. If the row says `present`, return `Pushed: false`. **Nothing transferred, no row written.** At 60 devices this is one indexed primary-key lookup instead of a four-minute USB transfer.
3. Open the blob and check its length against `farm.artifacts.size_bytes`. A store that has lost its bytes must fail before the ledger is told a push is under way.
4. Mark `pending`. A crash mid-push then leaves a row that says so, rather than no row at all.
5. Push, then record `present` or `failed`.

**A failed push does not end anything.** This package imports neither `internal/lease` nor `internal/adbwire` — verified, there are no `device-farmer/internal` imports in the package at all: the transfer arrives as a `PushFunc` supplied by the caller, so the store holds no socket, no transport and no device handle. On failure it records `failed` and returns an error naming itself retryable to a caller that still holds its lease and its device. A broken pipe halfway through a 200 MB push costs a retry, never a device. `recordFailure` runs on a **detached** context (`store.go:1014-1035`), because the case that most needs an accurate row is exactly the one where the caller's context is already dead; if even that write fails, the log is the only place the failure survives.

If the push succeeds but the ledger write fails, it reports `Pushed: true` with the write error. The bytes *are* on the device; the worst cost of a lost `present` is one redundant push next time.

**The skip trusts the ledger.** Anything that wipes a device — a medium or hard reset, a factory wipe, a reflash — **must** call `MarkRemoved` or `ForgetDevice`, or the next `EnsureOnDevice` will happily skip a push for content the device no longer holds.

One performance note that is really a lease note: `GET /api/v1/artifacts` counts the ledger once against a chosen page rather than with a correlated subquery. The ledger's primary key is `(device_id, sha256)` and there is no index on `sha256` alone, so the naive form re-scans it once per artifact returned: measured at 3 000 artifacts and 36 000 ledger rows that is **3.7 seconds** for `limit=2000` against 10 ms for this one (`internal/api/artifacts.go:426-438`). That is a tenant-role route, and the pool it would hold is the pool a holder borrows from to renew. A lease is never ended by a slow query, but a renewal that cannot get a connection is how one would be.

sections.heading: The APK metadata parser, and what it does when parsing fails
sections.body:
`farm.artifacts.package` and `version_code` are what let a spec say "the build of `com.acme.app` with version code ≥ 4711" instead of naming a path, and what let the runner decide whether an install is needed at all. Filling them means reading `AndroidManifest.xml` out of the APK.

The obvious tool is `aapt dump badging`. **The farm will not have it** — farmd runs in a container next to a USB hub, not on a machine with an Android SDK, and adding a 100 MB SDK plus an exec boundary to read four attributes is a bad trade. So the format is read directly: an APK is a zip, and `AndroidManifest.xml` inside it is AXML — Android's chunked binary XML with a string pool at the front. `ParseAXML` is the smallest reader that finds `package`, `versionCode`, `versionCodeMajor` and `versionName`, and stops at the first `<manifest>`. The entry lookup is case-sensitive: a zip entry called `androidmanifest.xml` is not the manifest, and treating it as one would let a crafted archive decide what package an artifact claims to be.

This is untrusted input arriving over an HTTP upload and parsed **inside the control plane**. A panic here takes down the process holding every lease in the farm. So: every multi-byte read goes through a bounds-checked primitive; every chunk size is refused unless it advances the cursor and stays inside the document, with the sum widened to int64 first so a wire value cannot wrap into a small positive offset; the decompressed manifest is capped at 8 MiB applied to the *stream*, not to the archive's own `UncompressedSize64` — which is exactly the field a hostile zip lies about; the string-pool offset table must *fit its chunk* before anything is allocated.

Attributes are matched on **both** the resource id and the name+namespace. Repackagers strip attribute names, the android namespace URI, or both; an id is proof of identity on its own because it is the compiled `android.R.attr` constant. `versionCode` outside `[0, 2^32-1]` and `versionCodeMajor` outside `[0, 2^31-1]` are discarded (`apk.go:262-268`) — a wide major shifted left by 32 wraps **negative**, which then sorts ahead of every genuine build in the `artifacts_pkg` index and quietly wins "latest build" queries.

**On failure the artifact is still stored.** `Put` reports the problem in `PutResult.ManifestErr`, logs it at WARN, and returns **201 Created** with a `manifest_error` field. Only `package` and `version_code` are missing; the content is stored and pushable. Reporting it as a failure would refuse every repackaged or obfuscated build in the fleet. `ctl push` prints the warning and exits 0.

sections.heading: GET /api/v1/capabilities — what this process will actually do
sections.body:
Unauthenticated, for the same reason `/healthz` is: an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state.

Every field is **observed, not declared**. Schema version comes from `goose_db_version`; each role's presence comes from its own heartbeat in `farm.component_heartbeat`; host agents come from `farm.hosts`; the auth mode comes from the `Authenticator` this server was actually built with. A feature list in a README describes what the project can do — this describes what this process, against this database, with this configuration, will do at 3am.

**This is the first thing to read on an unfamiliar farm**, because it is the only place the three not-built features are named together: `Authentication`, `Fence enforcement at the resource`, and `Helm chart`. The second of those is the one that changes how you read every other page: the fence is enforced in PostgreSQL and honoured by the client, and the mTLS proxy that would refuse a fenced connection at the ADB socket is not written.

The `roles` array names what each absence costs. On this farm `node` and `enroll` are both `running: false`, which is why the `Recovery ladder` feature reports *"No host agent is beating: tiers 3 and 4 are REFUSED with a reason, not silently skipped"* and `Dynamic enrollment` reports `unavailable`.

sections.heading: Metrics the surface emits
sections.body:
Nine series come from this layer — `farm_api_requests_total`, `farm_api_request_duration_seconds`, `farm_api_requests_in_flight`, `farm_api_stream_clients`, `farm_api_stream_clients_dropped_total`, `farm_api_stream_poll_errors_total`, `farm_api_device_execs_total`, `farm_api_operator_actions_total`, `farm_api_bulk_targets_total` — plus `farm_lease_renew_failures_total`, which the renewal handler raises through `internal/obs`. Two are worth an alert rule.

`farm_lease_renew_failures_total{kind="fenced"}` climbing means jobs are being aborted. `{kind="transient"}` climbing means the database is not answering renewals — **the leases are fine, the control plane is not**. Never alert on their sum.

`farm_api_operator_actions_total{action,outcome}` is the audit trail as a counter: `outcome="refused"` on `slot.power` or `artifact.delete` is the system working, not failing. `slot.power` also has `outcome="requested"` rather than `"ok"`, which is honest — the API recorded an intent, it did not switch anything.

sections.heading: Gaps closed since this page was written
sections.body:
The gap list below was written against an earlier tree, and part of it has since been fixed. Those entries are recorded here rather than deleted: a reader who remembers a gap needs to be able to tell **fixed** from **never there**, and the change that closed one is usually the shortest true description of what the behaviour is now.

The rule for this table is the rule for the gap list itself. An entry moves here only after the code was read and the claim checked against it, never because a commit message said so — which is exactly how the list went stale in the first place. Everything still open is in **What is not built here**, immediately below.

rows: The API was open and could not be closed by configuration. `cmd/farmd/roles.go` appended `api.WithAuthenticator(api.NewAllowAll(log, "anonymous"))` unconditionally, and `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv` — the function that reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` — had no caller, so the remedy `/api/v1/capabilities` printed did nothing.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go:187` now calls `api.AuthenticatorFor(cfg, log)`. It reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` and `FARM_API_AUTH`, builds a `StaticBearer`, and REFUSES to start an exposed listener with no credentials rather than booting open — an api that will not start is recorded as a control-plane gap and refunded onto every live lease, which booting open is not. `internal/api/auth_wiring.go`, with `internal/api/auth_test.go` behind it.

`farm.jobs.selector` was stored, validated, echoed by the API and never used for placement. `farm.lease_acquire` filtered on pool, admin_state, adb_state, health, slot state, rearm and `pin_device` only, so a job asking for `{"model":"Pixel 7"}` got whatever device was next in the ordering, with HTTP 200 where a working selector would have answered 409 no_capacity.

`migrations/00005_correctness.sql:181` adds `farm.device_matches`, and `lease_acquire` PHASE 2 calls it at line 330. The vocabulary is small and closed, and `farm.selector_unknown_keys` makes an unrecognised key a REFUSAL rather than an ignored line — silently dropping a constraint is how a job runs on hardware its author excluded on purpose.

Job step results were not exposed over the API at all. `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` returned exactly two keys, `job` and `leases`; `farm.job_steps` had no route, and the SSE `job` digest carried only ids and a state.

`GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/steps` and `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/attempts` (`internal/api/jobsteps.go`), tenant-scoped exactly as `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` is and writing nothing, plus `ctl job steps` and `ctl job attempts`.

There was no way to download an artifact's bytes over the API. `ArtifactAPI.Register` mounted five metadata routes; `Store.Get` and `Backend.Open` had no HTTP caller, and the `url` field was a `file://` path on the API host's own disk.

`GET /api/v1/artifacts/{sha}/content` (`internal/api/artifacts_blob.go`, mounted from `cmd/farmd/roles.go:172`). It serves through `http.ServeContent`, so ranged GETs work; the digest is in the path, so `Cache-Control: immutable` is a promise a content-addressed URL can honestly make; a missing or corrupt blob is a named error code rather than a 500.

`GET /api/v1/events` was farm-wide with no tenant scoping and no filters beyond `limit`, while `tenantScope` was applied in eight other places. Any tenant token — had tokens been wired — would have read every other tenant's job and device history, including operator `reason` text.

`internal/api/events_scope.go`. `handleEvents` builds an `EventScope`, clamps it to `tenantScope(r.Context())`, drops `farm.audit_log` entirely for a tenant-scoped caller, and echoes the scope in the response so a scoped list cannot read as the whole farm. It also adds the `kind`, `since` and `subject` filters the handler never had.

The API returned no 405. Because `mux.Handle("/api/v1/", …)` matched every path under the prefix, Go's method-mismatch handling never fired: a POST to a GET route came back `404 not_found` with no `Allow` header.

`internal/api/method.go` builds a method map at registration and `apiFallback` answers 405 with an `Allow` header, while a genuinely unknown path stays a 404 — answering 405 there would tell an unauthenticated caller which paths exist. `internal/api/method_test.go` covers both directions.

Recovery tiers 3 (`usb_reset`) and 4 (`port_power`) now have a client and a column to find an agent through, but no `node` role is beating on this deployment (`capabilities.roles[].running == false`), and the agent is Linux-only. Tiers 5 (`device_reboot`) and 7 (`adb_restart`) go over ADB and need only a reachable host.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go` builds a `node.NewClient` and passes it as the actuator's `HostRunner`, so tiers 3 and 4 reach `POST /node/v1/usb-reset` and `/port-power` instead of a nil runner refusing them. Two of nine rungs stopped being decorative. The agent on the far end is Linux-only and has still never faced hardware.

gaps.what: The fence is not enforced anywhere a device can be reached. `GET /api/v1/capabilities` reports feature "Fence enforcement at the resource" as `not_built`: "The mTLS proxy that would refuse a fenced connection at the ADB socket is not written" (`internal/api/capabilities.go:320-324`). No node/proxy binary exists in the tree. But `POST /api/v1/leases/{id}/revoke` returns, in its 200 body, "any socket still carrying fence 2329 is refused at the host proxy" (`internal/api/leases.go:718-722`), and `ctl lease revoke` prints the same sentence twice — once in its pre-flight warning and once in its result.
gaps.consequence: An operator who revokes a lease and reads only the HTTP reply or the ctl output will believe the previous holder has been cut off at the wire. It has not been. What actually happens is that `farm.devices.fence_floor` is raised, `farm.leases` marks the lease released, and the slot is quarantined for the rearm window (35 s here). A cooperating holder discovers this on its next renew, as a 410. A holder that is wedged, or one that simply does not renew before writing again, keeps an open ADB socket to a device that has been given away — and the only thing between it and the next job is the rearm timer. This is the same shape of exposure the whole design exists to prevent, at the one point where the design is still a promise. Treat slot rearm, not the fence, as the real barrier after a revoke, and size it accordingly.

gaps.what: An `install` step whose artifact push fails still aborts the rest of the job: the remaining steps are never created, and a job already written `succeeded` by another writer stays `succeeded`. What has changed is the abandoned bookkeeping — `internal/janitor` now closes the step and its attempt once the job's lease is no longer live, and re-queues or fails the job itself while it still reads `running`.
gaps.consequence: The API will still tell you a job succeeded when its APK never landed, if something other than the runner wrote that state — on this demo, the simulator does exactly that. The difference is that the step row no longer sits at `running` forever: it is closed as aborted with the sweeper named in its detail, so the contradiction is visible in the ledger instead of looking like an in-flight step. `farm.device_artifacts` remains the place the push failure itself is recorded. The janitor does not revisit a job that already left `running`, so a wrong terminal verdict is not corrected.

gaps.what: No blob garbage collection runs, although the sweep is written. `internal/api/artifacts_blob.go` implements `BlobGC` and `POST /api/v1/artifacts/gc` — dry run by default, a one-hour grace so it cannot race `Store.Put`'s commit-the-bytes-then-write-the-row window, a second reference check that fails closed, and a report naming any digest it lost a race for — and `internal/api/method_test.go` covers all of it. But `NewBlobGC` has no caller outside those tests: `runAPI` mounts `a.Register(mux)` and `a.RegisterBlobRoutes(mux)` (`cmd/farmd/roles.go:167-173`) and never constructs a `BlobGC`, so the route is not on the shipped binary. DELETE still removes the `farm.artifacts` row and retains the bytes (`blob_retained: true`), which remains the right answer for that request.
gaps.consequence: Disk under `$FARM_ARTIFACT_DIR` only grows on a farm built from this tree. Verified twice: after a successful DELETE the file was still present at `<tmp>/device-farmer-artifacts/b9/b94d27b9…`, and two blobs from an earlier session are on disk with no matching row. The design reasoning is sound — an unreferenced content-addressed blob is inert and gets adopted by the next identical upload — but reclaiming space is a manual `find` against `farm.artifacts` until the sweep is mounted, which is two lines in `runAPI` beside the ones that already mount the content route.

gaps.what: Tenant scoping stops at `/events`. `GET /api/v1/events` is scoped now (`internal/api/events_scope.go`, see the table above), but `/fleet`, `/topology`, `/hosts`, `/recovery`, `/bulk` and `/stream` are still farm-wide for every caller: `tenantScope` is called from `jobs.go`, `leases.go`, `artifacts.go` and `events_scope.go` and from nowhere else.
gaps.consequence: A tenant-scoped token reads every live lease's `lease_id`, `fence`, `job_id` and `tenant_id` from `/fleet` and from the SSE `lease` digest — the same exposure `handleLeaseRelease` documents as the reason release needs its own tenant check (`leases.go:441-458`). The stream is the hardest to fix: one shared poller produces one shared snapshot fanned out to every client, so scoping it means a poller per tenant.

gaps.what: `ctl bulk` overloads exit code 1: `bulkOutcome` (`internal/ctl/commands.go:2056-2061`) returns a failure whenever any target errored, in every output format, and ctl maps that onto the same exit code it uses when the control plane itself failed.
gaps.consequence: A bulk across 7 devices with 6 ok, 1 transport error and run state `done` exits 1: a script that treats 1 as "the control plane failed" will page on a single offline handset. Read the run's `ok/errors/skipped` counts instead. (The API half of this gap — no 405, ever — is closed; see the table above.)

gaps.what: The artifact routes are not tenant-scoped, and the new content route makes that consequential. `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{sha}/content` is mounted behind `requireRole(RoleTenant)` (`internal/api/artifacts_blob.go:262`) and `contentHandler` resolves the digest by sha alone — there is no `tenantScope` call on the path. `GET /api/v1/artifacts` filters on `kind` and `package` only (`internal/api/artifacts.go:402-420`), so the digests can be enumerated first. `tenantScope` appears exactly once in the artifact code, at `artifacts.go:518`, where it scopes the device REFERENCE list inside `handleGet` — the metadata, not the bytes.
gaps.consequence: A tenant token can list every digest in the farm and then download the full bytes of each: another tenant's APK, their harness, whatever they uploaded. Before the content route existed the cross-tenant exposure was metadata only — `handleGet` says as much, scoping the references while noting that the content itself is shared — and the new route escalates it to the artifact. `farm.artifacts` records a `tenant_id`, so the scoping is available and nothing applies it. If sharing content across tenants is deliberate, it is deliberate nowhere in writing, which is the same problem from the other direction.

verified:
All examples were run against the live system at http://127.0.0.1:8420 and postgres://farm@127.0.0.1:55432/device_farmer on 2026-09-04; every output block above is real, trimmed only for width. Roughly 118 commands.

HTTP probes: all 38 routes. GETs returning 200: /healthz, /readyz, /metrics, /api/v1/capabilities, /fleet, /devices/{id}, /topology, /hosts, /jobs, /jobs/{id}, /leases, /recovery, /bulk, /bulk/{id}, /events, /stream, /specs/kinds, /specs/resets?profile=default, /artifacts, /artifacts/{sha}, /devices/{id}/artifacts, /. Corrections found here: /specs/resets without ?profile= is 400 and with an unknown profile is 404 (both correct per specs.go:725-731); POST /specs/validate with an empty or non-object body is 400, NOT the "always 200" the draft claimed; POST /api/v1/bulk returns 202, not 201. Method mismatches are 404 in both directions with the method named, never 405; a bare /api/v1 is 307 to /api/v1/ which then 404s.

Lease lifecycle end to end: the demo's scheduler and job runner take over any queued job within about a second, so I parked a job (create, cancel, then acquire — farm.lease_acquire does not read jobs.state) to get a lease nothing else would touch. On lease dc010625 at fence 2329: renewed successfully (200, was_suspect false); renewed with a wrong fence (410 fenced); renewed with a wrong holder_instance (410 fenced, identical body); renewed with no fence (400); released with reason "device_offline" (400 check_violation, constraint leases_release_reason_check, seven permitted words returned) and with no reason (400) — then confirmed via /api/v1/leases that the lease was still held at fence 2329 with expires_in_s 900 and heartbeat_seq 1, untouched by four refusals; revoked it through `farmd ctl lease revoke --yes` (200, revoked fence 2329, new fence floor 2506) and confirmed the farm.audit_log row; revoked again (409 conflict), released it as its holder (200, released:false idempotent), revoked with no reason (400), revoked an unknown lease id (404). Also: acquire with an unknown job (404), acquire on a cancelled job (200 — a device was handed out), acquire with an unknown JSON field (400 invalid_json), a 1.2 MB body (413), a non-uuid job_id (400).

Operator routes: drained and undrained h01 and h02 (200 each; h01's drain reported live_leases 1 and the "nothing here releases them" note, h02's undrain carried no note), drain of an unknown host (404), drain with no reason (400); power-cycled slot 13 (202 accepted, attempt_id 94 — still open with no outcome minutes later), slot 22 (409 conflict, power_kind none), slot 16 (409 disruption_refused naming lease f9a404fe, job 7f3a6bac, tenant acme, policy allow_soft_reset, 7 slots in domain 3), slot 999999 (404), slot "abc" (400); exec on a free device by farm_uid (200, exit 0), on a leased device (409 naming the lease), with an empty command (400), on an unknown device (404); closed quarantine 5 (200) and closed it again (409), closed 9999 (404); ran a bulk across host=h01/hub=3-1 (202, then 7 targets, 5 ok, 1 error, 1 skipped-because-leased) and a bulk with a selector matching nothing (400).

Artifacts: re-uploaded the existing harness.apk (201, deduplicated:true, package com.acme.harness versionCode 40711 versionName 4.7.11); uploaded a plain zip as kind=apk and an 11-byte text file as kind=apk (both 201 with manifest_error "no AndroidManifest.xml" / "not a readable zip"); declared-digest mismatch (400 digest_mismatch, real received hash, nothing stored); invalid kind (400); missing name (400); malformed sha in path (400); unknown sha (404). DELETE of harness.apk was refused 409 naming 3 device ledger rows and 3 job specs; DELETE of the unreferenced b94d27b9 digest returned 200 blob_retained:true and the file was still on disk afterwards, with a follow-up GET and a second DELETE both 404. Two blobs from an earlier session (3a373c43…, 1245db57…) are on disk with no farm.artifacts row — the no-GC gap, on the floor.

SSE: captured 40 s of /api/v1/stream (230 655 bytes) — event names observed were exactly fleet (20), job (20), lease (15), recovery (6), alert (5), plus 1 `: connected` and 2 `: heartbeat` comment frames; verified the `retry: 3000` preamble and the Cache-Control / Connection / Content-Type / X-Accel-Buffering headers. Alert kinds seen live: hub_correlation, recovery_refused; all nine kinds confirmed against stream.go:719-894.

ctl (16 commands, all against the live API): help, fleet (plain and --host/--hub filtered), leases (table and -o json), hosts, recovery, artifacts, job, submit, validate, push, watch, device exec, bulk, lease revoke (pipe and --yes). Exit codes confirmed: 0 success, 1 transport failure (--url http://127.0.0.1:1), 2 usage (unknown command; revoke on a pipe without --yes), 3 remote refusal (revoke of an already-terminal lease). New finding: ctl bulk exits 1 when any target errored even though the run finished in state "done". ctl recovery shows all nine ladder rungs (0-8), not the five the draft printed.

Auth: sent a fabricated bearer token and a garbage Authorization header to /api/v1/fleet (200 both) and hit two operator-only routes with no credential (200/200), confirming AllowAll. Cross-checked by grepping the whole tree for AuthenticatorFromEnv / NewStaticBearer / WithAuthenticator call sites — the only production wiring is cmd/farmd/roles.go:148, and FARM_API_TOKENS appears only in auth.go's dead helper and in capabilities.go's advice string.

Database checks: farm.devices, farm.slots, farm.hubs, farm.power_domains, farm.quarantines, farm.leases, farm.jobs, farm.job_steps (which is where the succeeded-job-with-a-stuck-step gap reproduced), farm.device_artifacts, farm.artifacts, farm.audit_log, and the body of farm.lease_acquire in migrations/00002_lease.sql (to confirm the selector is never read and that re-attach overwrites holder_instance).

Invariant check: I re-read every section against "a lease ends when the job says so, when a deadline the user wrote down elapses, or when a human takes it back — nothing else." Nothing in the draft claimed or implied that a connectivity failure ends a lease, and nothing does now. Two passages were tightened rather than corrected: the 410 causes are now enumerated (released, reclaimed, re-attached by another acquire) so a reader cannot infer a network cause from "the lease is gone", and the exec, bulk and artifact-push failure paths now state explicitly what they leave untouched. The one place the invariant is weaker than it reads is the host proxy: the system's own words say a revoked holder is "refused at the host proxy", and no such proxy is built. That is recorded as gap 2 and flagged at every point where those words are quoted.

RE-VERIFIED GAP PASS. The gap list on this page was re-checked against the tree line by line after migrations 00005, 00006 and 00007 and the Go changes that came with them. Every entry moved into "Gaps closed since this page was written" was confirmed by reading the code that closed it, not by trusting a commit message. Three claims turned out to be stale in the other direction and were reopened: reaper.Collectors(), jobrunner.Collectors() and the recovery/node collectors are all still unregistered, because cmd/farmd/roles.go:86 calls obs.RegisterAll(reg, log) with no variadic groups and the only Collectors() call site in the tree sits in a branch farmd never takes. One claim was simply wrong when written — farm.slots.power_domain_id has existed since migrations/00001_core.sql:91 — and was corrected in place. Two claims about test coverage were narrowed rather than closed: internal/lease and internal/api are covered now; internal/reaper, internal/scheduler, internal/runner and internal/jobrunner still have zero test files. Only the six area JSON files were edited by this pass; no Go, SQL or UI code was touched. This pass also ADDED a gap the inventory never had: GET /api/v1/artifacts/{sha}/content is not tenant-scoped, and GET /api/v1/artifacts is not either, so a tenant token can enumerate every digest in the farm and download another tenant's bytes.
